title: Should Companies Be Allowed to Hack the Hackers?
summary:
Imagine if a store owner could chase down a thief instead of waiting for the police. That's kind of what President Trump wants to do with computer hackers! He signed a memo that could let some U.S. companies hack back at foreign cybercriminals—the bad guys who break into computers to steal money or information.

Usually, only government agencies like the FBI or NSA do that kind of work. But this new plan would let private businesses get permission to hack into the computer networks of foreign groups and mess them up. They could even destroy their systems!

There are rules, though. Companies would have to sign contracts with the Department of Justice or Homeland Security, go through "rigorous vetting," and set aside $1 million in case they mess up. But the memo doesn't explain exactly how targets would be chosen or what legal protections the companies would have.

Some people think this is a great idea. Joshua Steinman, who worked on cyber policy in Trump's first term, says there are lots of potential targets, like organized crime groups that do money laundering. He thinks many companies will see this as a chance to get government contracts and make money.

But others are worried. Paul Rosenzweig, a former homeland security official, thinks it's the wrong direction. He says private companies might be better at spying than actually stopping criminals, and there are still too many unanswered questions about legal authority.

The memo gives the government two months to figure out the details. So we'll have to wait and see if this "hack the hackers" plan actually happens!
why_it_matters: This matters because decisions about who can fight online criminals affect the safety of the computers, games, and private information your family uses every day.

background_read: President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) has pushed for stronger cyber defenses.
Normally, only government agencies such as the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) and NSA (National Security Agency) are allowed to break into foreign computer networks.
Countries and criminal groups often use hacking to steal money, spy on secrets, or disrupt computer systems, so governments try to decide who is allowed to fight back.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Trump signed the memo, and private U.S. companies could take part with oversight from the Department of Justice and Homeland Security.

WHAT: The plan would allow companies to hack back at foreign cybercriminals and even destroy their computer systems, but only after signing contracts, passing rigorous vetting, and setting aside $1 million.
WHERE: The action happens in the United States, targeting foreign groups.

WHY: Supporters say it could stop organized crime and create government contracts, while critics warn about legal authority and the risk that companies may be better at spying than stopping criminals.

perspectives.description: They think the plan creates many possible targets, such as organized crime groups, and will attract companies that want government contracts.
They worry private companies may be good at spying but not at stopping criminals, and that legal authority is still unclear.
Because the memo gives the government two months to work out the details, many people are waiting to see what the final rules will be before deciding what is safe.
